background.definition: Burns are tissue injuries caused by heat (thermal), friction, chemicals, electricity, or irradiation. This chapter will only cover thermal burns.

list.listitem: An estimated 500,000 burn injuries receive medical treatment every year in the United States, with 40,000 hospitalizations.
There are an estimated 4000 burn deaths per year in United States.
Fire/flame (46%)
Scald (32%)
Hot object contact (8%)
Electrical (4%)
Chemical (3%)
Other (6%)

Burn severity is related to the total amount of heat transfer, which is dependent on the burn agent's temperature, duration of contact, transfer coefficient, heat capacity, and the size of exposed area.

Local responses include hyperemia, stasis, and coagulation. These local responses induce the release of cytokines and multiple inflammatory mediators, which may cause severe systemic responses including increased capillary permeability causing edema and intravascular fluid loss, bronchospasm, decreased myocardial contractility, increased basal metabolic rate and nonspecific immunological response delay.
Evidence suggests the WHO Safe Communities model is effective in reducing injuries in whole populations. B
Limited evidence exists on the effectiveness of community-based injury-prevention programs to prevent burns and scalds in children. B
Counseling as part of child health surveillance may increase smoke alarm ownership and use, but its effects on fire-related injuries are unevaluated. B
Assess patients with basic life support measures, and then assess the severity of the burn by estimating its depth and size. C
Obtain basic laboratory tests (CBC, electrolyte levels, renal function, UA, type and cross for blood products) and a chest x-ray, if needed. C
Laser Doppler is not an established method to measure the depth of a burn. B
Evaluate burn size and depth to determine whether to refer to a burn center ( and ). C

Response to topical antibiotics, unclear burn history
Pruritus, rapid spread from small lesion, common on face

list.listitem: See .
Identify the source of burn (e.g., fire, hot water, electricity, chemicals) and remove patient from further contact.
Expose and inspect the full body during physical examination.
Assess airway involvement, by examining for facial burns, carbon particles in nares or oropharynx, or carbon-stained sputum. Careful auscultation of the upper airway to lungs is important.

Assess the size and depth of the burn, and document it. Check skin for color, blister, moist/dry, blanching, and pain sensation. The estimated body surface area can be calculated by using the Rule of Nines ().

Consider differential diagnosis if there is an unclear history or presentation (i.e., blistering diseases). Consider abuse in children, any patients with unreasonable history, and in patients with typical physical characteristics (e.g., doughnut sign in buttock).

In a systematic review, features of intentional scald injuries were immersion injuries affecting the extremities, buttocks or perineum or both that were symmetrical with clear upper margins, and were associated with old fractures and unrelated injuries. Unintentional scalds were more commonly from hot liquid spills and affected the upper body with irregular margins and depth.
Initial basic laboratory tests include CBC, electrolyte levels, renal function, type and cross for blood products, and UA.
Order a chest x-ray if inhalation is possible and creatinine phosphokinase for patients with full-thickness burns or patients with partial-thickness burns who need IV fluid resuscitation.
Consider an arterial blood gas test and carboxyhemoglobin level if airway involvement or smoke inhalation is suspected.
Laser Doppler is not an established method of burn depth measurement.
Use eschar/full-thickness biopsy instead of wound culture to assess for infection.
Evaluate for airway involvement: check for facial burn, carbon particle in nostril or oropharynx, or carbon-stained sputum. Auscultate upper airway to lungs.
Identify the source of burn (e.g., fire, hot objects/water, chemical, electrical), then remove it if attached. Assess size, depth, and location of burn (see and ).
Assess other risk factors (e.g., comorbidity, physical function baseline, concerns of abuse).
Refer to a burn center if patient meets the criteria in .
If outpatient management: (1) pain management, (2) wound care (initial debridement, wound dressing), and (3) infection control with topical antimicrobial.
Perform frequent follow-ups and refer early if concerns of aesthetic or functional disturbance arise.
Provide adequate pain control. C
Skin can be cooled with room temperature or slightly cool water to provide some initial pain relief for no more than 5 minutes (to avoid maceration). Ice or iced water is not recommended.
Fluid resuscitation is indicated if 20% or more body surface area is involved (4 mL/kg/percent of burn to body surface area; half in initial 8 hours, remaining half in next 16 hours). C
Manage blisters; debride with dressing by biologic, biosynthetic, or synthetic materials under controlled moist environment. C
Dress the burn daily with topical antimicrobials such as polysporin, mafenide acetate, or silver nitrate for deep partial-thickness and full-thickness burns. C
Consider referral to a burn center if patient meets the criteria in . C
Adequate pain control is important. Oral analgesics, such as acetaminophen or NSAIDs, are sufficient for most burns.
Narcotics may be necessary for severe partial-thickness burns or with dressing changes, as needed.

Fluid resuscitation is indicated if 20% or more of the body surface area is involved: 4 mL of lactated Ringer's solution or normal saline per kilogram of body weight per percent of burn body surface area. Give half in the initial 8 hours, the remaining half in the next 16 hours. Optimal resuscitation fluid choice has not been established by sufficient evidence.
Update tetanus immunization, if necessary. Consider prophylaxis for peptic ulcers. Systemic antibiotics should be used only for suspected or proven burn infections.
Gabapentin and pregabalin can be used as adjunctive therapy for pain control and post-burn pruritus.

A Cochrane review on intravenous lidocaine for pain relief in people with burns "... found one small clinical trial, involving only 45 participants, which showed a benefit from intravenous lidocaine for pain relief in people with burns. The trial did not show a difference in opioid use, participant anxiety or level of participant satisfaction with the use of intravenous lidocaine."
Debride burn of necrotic or sloughed skin prior to applying topical antimicrobial treatment to increase effectiveness.

Dress the burn with topical antimicrobials such as mafenide acetate, bacitracin, nanocrystalline silver, or silver nitrate for deep partial-thickness and full-thickness burns. Mupirocin can be used if MRSA is suspected.
Though commonly used, topical silver sulfadiazine cream appears to result in slower wound healing than newer dressings for minor burns.
In addition, a recent meta-analysis comparing nanocrystalline silver to older silver formulations demonstrated a significantly reduced incidence of infection (9.5% vs. 26.8%, respectively).

Ruptured blisters should be debrided. Do not deroof blisters if they are likely to rupture imminently or occur in a location where they are likely to rupture (e.g., leg, joints). Aspiration of intact blisters is not recommended because of an increased risk of infection associated with the procedure. Large blisters (>6 mm) should be debrided, because they are likely to rupture spontaneously. Debridement of large blisters will help to reduce mechanical pressure on underlying tissue and exposure of wound bed to blister fluid, which contains substances the suppress immune response and may impede healing.

A randomized controlled trial of 40 patients with burn-related blisters greater than 6 mm were randomized to blister management by draining or deroofing. There were no difference in the number of days to complete wound healing between the 2 groups, however there were trends toward the aspiration group demonstrating improvements in scars and pain.

A controlled moist healing environment should be provided on debrided partial-thickness burns wound with biosynthetic (e.g., Biobrane, TransCyte, Mepitel, DuoDERM), biologic (e.g., human allograft, pigskin), or synthetic dressing to optimize healing, decrease scarring, minimize dressing change requirements, and provide patient comfort, without increased rates of infection.
Use escharotomy in constricting circumferential burns of extremities or trunk.
Use skin graft or artificial skin substitute for full-thickness burns in selected cases.
Negative pressure closure technique in the split-thickness skin graft diminishes the loss of graft area and shortens the days of hospital stay.
Honey appears to heal partial thickness burns more quickly (perhaps by 4-5 days) than other conventional treatments. Conclusions about other outcomes are limited by low quality evidence.
Aloe vera appears to be effective in reducing healing time in patients with first or second degree burns and its use is associated with accelerated healing of split-thickness skin graft donor sites.

In a prospective, single blind controlled trial among 40 patients with burn scar pain, extracorporeal shock wave therapy (ESWT) significantly reduced scar pain in burn patients after wound epithelialization compared to sham ESWT plus standard therapy (medication, physical therapy and burn rehabilitation massage therapy).
Cold pack therapy may be effective in reducing post-burn pruritis.
Early mobilization, pain control, and follow-up functional evaluations are important.

American Burn Association guidelines (2024) recommend consideration of use of albumin solution in patients with larger burns to reduce fluid resuscitation volumes. They also recommend beginning fluid resuscitation with 2 ml/kg/% total body surface area. They found insufficient evidence regarding use of high-dose vitamin C, fresh frozen plasma,vasopressors, or early continuous renal replacement therapy.
There is insufficient evidence to support or refute the effectiveness of hyperbaric oxygen therapy for the management of thermal burns.

There is insufficient evidence to support or refute the effectiveness of early vs. late enteral nutrition support in adults with burn injury, but a high-carbohydrate, high-protein, low-fat enteral feeding may be preferable over a low-carbohydrate, high-protein, high-fat enteral feeding.
Consider appropriate referral to burn center using criteria in .

Consider treatment of keloids for functional or aesthetic indications. A combination of liquid nitrogen cryotherapy and corticosteroid intradermal injection is usually effective to reduce the problem. Liquid nitrogen is thoroughly applied to the keloid, then 5 minutes later methylprednisolone 40 mg/mL can be infiltrated to the keloid intradermally. This treatment can be repeated every 6 weeks for better results.
Weak evidence exists to support the use of silicon gel sheeting/bandages for hypertrophic scarring and keloids, though higher quality studies are needed.
Although evidence is limited, the use of pressure garment therapy does not appear to improve global scar scores.

A clinical rule uses burn size of more than 40% of body surface area, age older than 60 years, and presence of inhalation injury to predict survival after burn. Patient mortality is 0.3% with no risk factors, 3% with 1 risk factor, 33% with 2 risk factors, and approximately 90% with all 3 risk factors. B
A second clinical rule was developed and validated by Belgian investigators.
Oxandrolone and exercise may be beneficial in severely burned children, but the evidence is not strong.

There is evidence from one RCT to support the long-term use of growth hormone in severely burned children (>40% body surface area) to improve growth and lean body mass. There was a slight decrease in bone mineral density and cardiac output of unknown consequence.

feature.caption: Classification of Burns.
feature.feature_body:
Depth Anatomy Characteristics
Superficial burn Epidermis only Painful, dry, red but blanching with pressure. No blister. No scarring
Partial-thickness, superficial Superficial dermis Painful, moist, red but blanching with pressure. Blister. Rare scarring
Partial-thickness, deep Deep dermis Painful, wet, red and not blanching with pressure. Blister. Scarring
Full-thickness Entire dermis to SC damage Painless, white/gray to black in color, dry. Scarring. Contractures

feature.caption: Criteria for Burn Center Referral.
feature.feature_body: Partial-thickness burns of greater than 10% of the total body surface area Burns that involve the face, hands, feet, genitalia, perineum, or major joints Third-degree burns in any age group Electrical burns, including lightning injury Chemical burns Inhalation injury Burn injury in patients with preexisting medical disorders that could complicate management, prolong recovery, or affect mortality Any patients with burns and concomitant trauma (such as fractures) in which the burn injury poses the greatest risk of morbidity or mortality. In such cases, if the trauma poses the greater immediate risk, the patient's condition may be stabilized initially in a trauma center before transfer to a burn center. Physician judgment will be necessary in such situations and should be in concert with the regional medical control plan and triage protocols Burned children in hospitals without qualified personnel or equipment for the care of children Burn injury in patients who will require special social, emotional, or rehabilitative intervention Excerpted from Guidelines for the Operation of Burn Centers (pp. 79-86), Resources for Optimal Care of the Injured Patient 2006, Committee on Trauma, American College of Surgeons.
